title: CI and Frontend Deployment
summary: A team needs repeatable steps to check and publish a website.

subtopics.title: Continuous integration
subtopics.explanation: Continuous integration (CI) runs shared checks when code changes. It can install locked dependencies, check types, run tests, and build the site. It is like inspecting each batch before it leaves a workshop. A failing check should show which change needs attention. For example, a pull request can run type checking and tests before someone approves it. In practice, run checks on the same locked dependencies that developers use locally.

subtopics.title: Build output
subtopics.explanation: A production build turns source files into browser-ready output, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript chunks, and images. It is like packing the final product for delivery. Test that output because development mode can behave differently and hide deployment problems. For example, a production build may reveal missing environment values that a development server supplied automatically. In practice, keep preview deployments separate so a test release cannot overwrite production data.

subtopics.title: Deployment
subtopics.explanation: Deployment publishes a known build to a hosting environment. Connect the release to a commit or build identifier so a team can tell exactly what users received. It is like putting a batch number on a shipped product. Verify routes, assets, and runtime settings after release. For example, a release identifier lets support connect a report to the exact files deployed. In practice, record the build ID or commit hash next to release health signals.

subtopics.title: Secrets and settings
subtopics.explanation: Preview and production environments may use different settings. Secret values belong in protected hosting configuration, never in client bundles or committed files. It is like keeping a key in a locked office rather than printing it on the package. Check which variables are public before a build. For example, store an API secret in the host settings and keep it out of browser bundles. In practice, use a secret manager for credentials and expose only public configuration to the browser.

subtopics.title: Rollback
subtopics.explanation: A rollback returns traffic to a known-good release. Keep the recovery steps clear and make sure older pages can still load their assets. It is like switching back to the last working version of a tool. Practice the rollback before an incident, not during the first outage. For example, a rollback should restore a known build, not rebuild an unknown old branch during an outage. In practice, verify that rollback includes compatible static assets and not only the server process.

foundations.overview: Continuous integration and deployment help teams check and release frontend changes reliably. CI runs repeatable checks; a production build creates files for users; deployment publishes a known build. Think of it like inspecting a package, preparing it, then delivering a labeled version. Keep secrets out of browser code and have a tested rollback path when a release causes trouble.
foundations.whyItMatters: CI and deployment make the path from code to users repeatable. A known build, protected settings, and recovery process lower release risk and speed incident response.
foundations.browserPerspective: A CI pipeline runs outside a user’s browser, then serves build output from a host or CDN.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use repeatable checks for pull requests and deploy a build that passed them.
foundations.businessImpact: Reliable releases reduce user impact and shorten recovery from mistakes.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Keep environment settings and release identities clear across preview and production.
foundations.performanceImpact: Cache build artifacts safely and measure the effect of deployment changes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: CI proves the product has no bugs
commonMisconceptions.reality: Checks cover selected risks; production monitoring and review still matter.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A successful build means deployment is correct
commonMisconceptions.reality: The host, environment variables, redirects, and cache rules can still be wrong.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A green CI run proves every user journey works.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Automated checks cover only the cases they exercise; monitor real releases and test critical flows.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A deployment is complete when files upload.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Verify routes, assets, runtime settings, and error signals after traffic reaches the release.

keyTakeaways: Continuous integration (CI) runs shared checks when code changes.
A production build turns source files into browser-ready output, such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript chunks, and images.
Deployment publishes a known build to a hosting environment.
Preview and production environments may use different settings.
A rollback returns traffic to a known-good release.
